title: Death and return
hookLine: the soul is drawn out and returns to its Lord

lines: THE FIRST WORDS, AT THE LAST.
cards: A hospital room, late. The machines hum. Around the bed, a family speaks softly, and someone leans close to the person lying there and says, gently, la ilaha illa Allah.
There is no god but God. They aren't asking for anything. They are reminding.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim tells Muslims to do exactly this: prompt your dying to say la ilaha illa Allah. So the last words hoped for at that bed are the first words of the faith.

teach.h: NEARER THAN THOSE AROUND THE BED.
teach.b: Day 686 called death a return; today, the moment itself. The word is mawt, death, and the Qur'an slows down for it.

In Surah al-Waqi'ah, it describes the soul rising to the throat while the people around the bed look on, and adds, in paraphrase: and We are nearer to him than you, though you do not see. The family is close.
Allah, the verse says, is closer. Then a long hadith, narrated by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and collected by Imam Ahmad, with a shorter version in Abu Dawud, tells it as a scene. Angels come to the dying.

teach.h: DRAWN OUT LIKE A DROP FROM A WATER SKIN.
teach.b: For the believer, they come with bright faces, and the soul is drawn out gently, the hadith says, the way a drop flows from the mouth of a water skin.
For the one who turned away, it is described as hard, like a skewer pulled through wet wool. The scene is read as both comfort and warning. And then the direction.
Death in the Qur'an is not a disappearing; it is a going back.

In Surah al-Fajr the soul at rest is addressed, and Pickthall gives it like this: "But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure!" The soul came from somewhere, and it is called home.
That's why a hadith in Tirmidhi tells Muslims to remember death often, calling it the destroyer of pleasures. Not to be gloomy, but to keep the pleasures in their place.
Someone who remembers they are going back tends to pack more carefully.

how: When a Muslim is dying, family often sit close and gently remind them of the shahada, la ilaha illa Allah, and on hearing of a death Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to Allah and to Him we return.

o: death, when the soul is drawn out and returns to its Lord
the grave, the in-between from dying until the Day
the angel sent to ask the dead their three questions

games.q: death and return — tap the pairs.
p: the soul like a drop from a water skin

s: Muslims are told never to think about death
a hadith in Tirmidhi says to remember death often, the destroyer of pleasures.
in al-Fajr, the soul at peace is told to return to its Lord
"Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure!"
at the bedside, a hadith tells Muslims to prompt the dying to say la ilaha illa Allah
the first words of the faith become the last words hoped for.

games.q: you're sitting beside someone you love who is dying. by the hadith in Sahih Muslim, what do you say?
o: gently prompt them: la ilaha illa Allah.
read them a long list of their good deeds.
games.why: the hadith says: prompt your dying to say la ilaha illa Allah. the first words of the faith, softly, at the last.

practice: If this is too heavy today, stop here and simply breathe; that's allowed.

Otherwise, notice the breath going out and the small pause before it comes back, hold lightly the thought that one day it won't, and ask: if I were called back today, what would I want to have done this week?
If you pray, say quietly, la ilaha illa Allah, or rest on the word return; and if dark thoughts come and stay, in the US call or text 988, any hour, or elsewhere, local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Mawt. Death: in Muslim teaching, the soul drawn out and returning to its Lord. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: return. A new part begins here: the unseen journey. That's today, done.
